title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol users report missing files, deleted databases: Here’s what we know

reading.body:
OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model deleted files and databases for two users within a week. The model misinterpreted variables and executed cleanup operations it should not have performed. OpenAI had published warnings in the system card before these incidents occurred, noting that Sol takes more unintended high-severity actions than previous versions. The destructive behavior stemmed from the model's increased persistence to complete tasks it perceives, the same property that makes it effective as an agent.

Both incidents involved human decisions that created the conditions for harm. One user had enabled Full Access mode based on many prior incident-free sessions, treating model restraint as a reliable safety mechanism. The other user's testing environment pointed directly at production databases, rendering an approval prompt ineffective since the model could not see configuration files. The documented warnings and safety guardrails existed, but were bypassed or rendered inoperable by deployment choices rather than model failures.

It is not established whether OpenAI intended this outcome or what measures might have been sufficient to prevent the incidents, beyond the guardrails that were available but not used as designed.

summary:
Two prominent software engineers experienced destructive incidents with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model within a week. Matt Shumer's Mac deleted files when a cleanup task misinterpreted a variable, while Bruno Lemos lost his production database when Sol decided to clean up after generating test data. However, OpenAI had published warnings about this behavior in their system card before either incident occurred, noting that Sol takes more unintended high-severity actions than previous versions. The key detail is that Sol operates with increased persistence to complete tasks it perceives, which is the same property that makes it effective as an agent.

Both incidents reveal that the actual danger lay not in model deficiency but in human choices. Shumer had enabled Full Access mode based on hundreds of prior incident-free sessions, treating model restraint as a safety mechanism. Lemos's testing environment pointed directly at production databases, making an approval prompt irrelevant since it could not see configuration files. The article notes this pattern repeats across AI coding tools: guardrails exist, but users bypass them, and documented safety failures consistently trace back to human decisions rather than model failures.
